name: Bamus
title: Bamus Volcano (South Son): Last Eruption, Height & Location
description: Bamus, the “South Son” beside Ulawun on New Britain, last erupted about {last_year}. What was seen there in 2006, the 1990 earthquakes, its height and its record.
since_check: **Not erupting.** The Smithsonian’s list, updated to November 15, 2026, has no eruption of Bamus since about {last_year}, and its newest report on the volcano describes July 12, 2006: white vapor from the summit, no ash.[[gvp]] No alert level and no statement of the Rabaul Volcano Observatory about Bamus were found when the sources were read, on {read_date}.
lede: Bamus is the quiet neighbor of Ulawun, one of the most active volcanoes on the island of New Britain in Papua New Guinea. The two are the highest volcanoes of the Bismarck arc, and an old story of the Nakanai people makes Bamus the son of Ulawun. Its last eruption came about {quiet_number} years ago. Below: where it is, what has been reported since, when it last erupted, how it got its name, its height, and every eruption on record.
answer: **Bamus last erupted about {last_year}**, give or take {last_margin} years, on the Smithsonian’s list.[[gvp]] It is a **stratovolcano** on New Britain in Papua New Guinea, **{summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m)** high, southwest of the more active Ulawun.[[gvp]] The newest report on it dates from July 2006, when people watched white vapor rise from the summit for about an hour and a half; no ash fell.[[gvp]]

paras: Bamus is on New Britain, the largest island of the Bismarck Archipelago in [Papua New Guinea](/volcanoes-in-papua-new-guinea), at {coords}.[[gvp]][[nasa]]

It stands southwest of [Ulawun](/volcano/ulawun), the tallest volcano on the island.[[nasa]] The seismograph at Ulawun that followed the earthquakes under Bamus in 1990 was about 16 miles (25 km) away.[[gvp]]
Bamus is one of {n_country} volcanoes in Papua New Guinea on the Smithsonian’s Holocene list; [Langila](/volcano/langila) and [Manam](/volcano/manam) are two of the others.[[gvp]]

Bamus is not erupting. Its last eruption on the Smithsonian’s list is dated to about {last_year}, give or take {last_margin} years, and the Smithsonian’s page has no report of an eruption since.[[gvp]]

The newest report is from 2006. On July 12 of that year people saw white vapor rising from the summit from about 10:10 a.m. Around 11:10 the emission grew forceful and took on a slight gray tint. The plume drifted south-southeast, no ash fall was reported, and satellites picked up no heat at the volcano.[[gvp]]

Those who watched included local government officials from Bialla, an observer from the mining department, and a man at a resort 25 to 30 miles (40 to 50 km) away, who phoned the Rabaul Volcano Observatory. The Smithsonian’s report gives no verdict from the observatory and does not call the event an eruption.[[gvp]]

The earlier report is about earthquakes. They began on February 2, 1990 with almost 100 events. Between February 10 and 15 instruments counted about 1,400, three of them of magnitude 5.8 to 6.0, and between February 25 and 28 about 880 more. Their centers lined up in a zone about 6 miles (10 km) long that took in the south flanks of Bamus, at depths down to 14 miles (23 km).[[gvp]]

Inspections on February 13 and 16 found rockfalls in many places on the volcano and the steam vents on the summit dome no warmer than 59 °F (15 °C). A month later the cause was still uncertain.[[gvp]]

Papua New Guinea’s volcanoes are the responsibility of the Rabaul Volcano Observatory. A directory entry of the World Organization of Volcano Observatories, undated and written no earlier than 2002, lists observation posts at four volcanoes: Ulawun, Langila, Manam and Karkar. Bamus is not among them.[[wovo]]
In February 1990 a temporary network of seismographs was set up for four days. After that the permanent seismograph at Ulawun followed the earthquakes.[[gvp]]

A document about the observatory on the disaster-risk site PreventionWeb, written no earlier than 2014, says that it monitored only seven of the country’s 15 active volcanoes, for want of money, staff and equipment. It does not name the seven.[[pw]] This page found no website of the observatory itself and no alert level for Bamus.

About {quiet_number} years ago. The Smithsonian’s list dates the last eruption to {last_year}, give or take {last_margin} years, from what people reported, and rates it 3 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI), with a question mark.[[gvp]]

Nobody recorded it as it happened. By the Smithsonian’s summary, residents describe an eruption in the late 19th century, and young deposits of pyroclastic flows lie on the volcano’s flanks.[[gvp]] A NASA caption to a 2012 astronaut photograph of the two volcanoes says the same: Bamus was last active in the late 19th century.[[nasa]]

A sketch may show the volcano at work. In 1878, the earliest year in the Smithsonian’s range, the English explorer Wilfred Powell drew Ulawun and Bamus from Lolobau Island, each with a plume of vapor. A history of the region’s eruptions counts that as possible evidence that Bamus was active in 1878 and calls it not conclusive: the plume held little or no ash, and Powell’s observations include mistakes and exaggeration.[[john3]]
Powell also reported the summit bare. Today Bamus is covered in vegetation.[[john3]][[gvp]]

sections.h: Why is Bamus called the South Son?
paras: The name is Powell’s. He named three volcanoes the Father, the South Son and the North Son: Ulawun, Bamus and Likuruanga.[[john3]] The Smithsonian still lists South Son and Sudsohn as other names for Bamus.[[gvp]]

The names follow a story of the Nakanai people, published in 1909. Ulawun, a stranger who came down from the mountain smoking tobacco, married a Nakanai woman, Simolo. Their son was told to find a home of his own. He settled on a nearby mountain and gave it his name, Bamus.[[john3]]
In the story the son took after the father: Bamus, too, smoked, breathed fire and threw up stones, and people in the valleys were killed.[[john3]]

Bamus is {summit_ft} ft ({summit_m} m) above sea level.[[gvp]] Ulawun, next to it, is 7,657 ft (2,334 m), and the two are the highest volcanoes of the Bismarck volcanic arc, a chain about 620 miles (1,000 km) long.[[nasa]][[gvp]]
It rises about {rise_ft} ft ({rise_m} m) above the land around it, which lies at about {ground_ft} ft ({ground_m} m).[[etopo]]

sections.h: What type of volcano is Bamus?
paras: The Smithsonian lists Bamus as a stratovolcano whose main rock is {rock}.[[gvp]] It is a symmetrical cone covered in rainforest.[[gvp]]

The crater at the summit is broken open and filled by a lava dome. A smaller cone sits on the south flank, and halfway up the southeast flank there is a crater about 0.9 miles (1.5 km) wide with two small cones beside it.[[gvp]]

sections.note: This page is a record, not a safety guide. For current warnings, follow the Rabaul Volcano Observatory and Papua New Guinea’s disaster authorities.
paras: Nothing in its record says it is finished. The Smithsonian’s list has {n_all} eruptions of Bamus since about {oldest}, the last about {quiet_number} years ago, and the deposits of pyroclastic flows on its flanks are young.[[gvp]]

The history of the region’s eruptions cited above calls Bamus a “sleeper.” It gives four examples, Savo, Bamus, Makalaia-Dakataua and Victory, all last active in the nineteenth century, and judges each capable of an eruption larger than its last.[[john16]]
NOAA’s database of significant eruptions has no entry for Bamus.[[noaa]]
The Smithsonian’s record for Bamus has **{n_all} confirmed eruptions**: {n_rc_word} dated by radiocarbon and one known from reports. It gives none of them an end date.[[gvp]]

calc: **{quiet_number} {quiet_unit} ago:** this year minus {last_year}, rounded to the nearest {quiet_round} years. The Smithsonian dates the last eruption to {last_year} with a margin of {last_margin} years either way, so a count to the year would claim more than is known.

**about {rise_ft} ft ({rise_m} m):** the summit height minus the height of the land around the volcano, {ground_m} m. That is the median height of the land 14 to 16 km from the summit in NOAA’s ETOPO 2022 grid, rounded to 50 m; about one cell in sixteen of that ring is sea and is left out.
Feet and miles are converted from the metric figures in the sources and rounded, and the temperature from degrees Celsius.
